items.prompt: A checkout page shows 'Recommended for you' next to a product, based on the user's actual past purchases. Is this persuasive design or a dark pattern?
choices: A dark pattern, because it's trying to influence what the user buys
Persuasive design, because it's true, relevant information that helps the decision, and the influence doesn't degrade the user's ability to choose freely
A dark pattern, because any personalization is manipulative by definition
Neither, because recommendations never actually change behavior
items.explanation: The dividing line isn't whether something tries to influence a choice — almost all design does. It's whether the influence works by giving the user true, relevant information (persuasion) or by hiding information, exploiting a bias, or creating asymmetric effort (manipulation). An accurate recommendation based on real purchase history informs; it doesn't degrade the user's ability to choose.
items.reference:
Persuasive

True, relevant info; both sides roughly benefit

Manipulative

Hidden/false info, or a bias exploited at the user's expense

Why: the test is whether influence informs the choice or degrades the user's ability to make it freely — not whether influence exists at all.

items.prompt: A site displays 'Only 2 left in stock!' on every product page, regardless of actual inventory, which is never actually low. What makes this manipulative rather than persuasive?
choices: Nothing — urgency messaging is always a legitimate design technique
It's false and irrelevant to the real decision — it exploits urgency bias with information that doesn't reflect reality, purely to rush a decision
It's manipulative only if the product is expensive
It's fine as long as the checkout process itself is fast
items.explanation: A real 'low stock' notice would be persuasive (true, relevant information). A fabricated one that never reflects actual inventory fails the truth test outright — it exploits urgency bias with information that has no basis in fact, purely to rush a decision the user might not otherwise make as quickly.
items.reference:
Persuasive

True, relevant info; both sides roughly benefit

Manipulative

Hidden/false info, or a bias exploited at the user's expense

Why: the test is whether influence informs the choice or degrades the user's ability to make it freely — not whether influence exists at all.

items.prompt: Which single question best separates ordinary persuasive design from a dark pattern?
choices: Does the design try to change what the user does?
Does the influence work by informing the user better, or by degrading their ability to choose freely?
Does the design use color or animation to draw attention?
Does the design increase the business's revenue?
items.explanation: Nearly all design tries to influence behavior — that alone doesn't make it manipulative. The dividing line is the mechanism: informing the user better (persuasion) versus degrading their ability to choose freely through hidden info, false urgency, or asymmetric effort (manipulation).
items.reference:
Persuasive

True, relevant info; both sides roughly benefit

Manipulative

Hidden/false info, or a bias exploited at the user's expense

Why: the test is whether influence informs the choice or degrades the user's ability to make it freely — not whether influence exists at all.

items.prompt: A free trial silently converts to a paid subscription with no clear advance warning, charging the user's card automatically. Which dark-pattern family is this?
choices: Roach motel
Forced continuity
Trick questions
Nagging
items.explanation: Forced continuity is when a free or trial offer silently converts into a paid, recurring charge without a clear, well-timed warning. It's distinct from roach motel (easy in, hard out) — forced continuity is specifically about the transition from free to paid happening without real notice.
items.reference:
Roach motelEasy in, hard out
ConfirmshamingGuilt-trips the 'no' label
Forced continuitySilent free-to-paid conversion

Why: each family exploits a different mechanism — matching the mechanism to the name is what makes the pattern nameable, and therefore fixable.

items.prompt: A checkout flow's final page reveals a $12 'service fee' that wasn't shown anywhere earlier in the process. Which dark-pattern family is this?
choices: Hidden costs
Nagging
Roach motel
Confirmshaming
items.explanation: Hidden costs specifically means the real total cost is revealed only at the last possible step, after the user has already invested effort into the flow and is less likely to abandon it. This differs from forced continuity (a later silent charge) and roach motel (difficulty exiting).
items.reference:
Roach motelEasy in, hard out
ConfirmshamingGuilt-trips the 'no' label
Forced continuitySilent free-to-paid conversion

Why: each family exploits a different mechanism — matching the mechanism to the name is what makes the pattern nameable, and therefore fixable.

items.prompt: What does the 'roach motel' pattern specifically describe?
choices: A design that's ugly or outdated
A flow that's easy to enter but disproportionately hard to exit
A page that loads slowly
A form with too many required fields
items.explanation: Roach motel names the asymmetry between getting in and getting out — signing up, subscribing, or opting in takes little effort, while the reverse action is buried, multi-step, or requires a phone call. The name comes from the old pest-trap slogan: 'roaches check in, but they don't check out.'
items.reference:
🖱️1 click in
→
🧭🧭🧭4+ screens out

Why: the effort asymmetry itself — not any single screen — is what makes a roach motel a dark pattern.

items.prompt: A loyalty program can be joined with one tap at checkout, but deleting the account requires calling a phone number only staffed on weekday business hours. What pattern is this?
choices: Nagging
Roach motel
Trick questions
Persuasive design — phone support is a normal service
items.explanation: This is roach motel applied to account deletion rather than a subscription: near-zero effort to join, disproportionate and inconvenient effort to leave (a business-hours-only phone call vs. a one-tap signup). The presence of a phone number doesn't make it legitimate — the asymmetry is the issue.
items.reference:
🖱️1 click in
→
🧭🧭🧭4+ screens out

Why: the effort asymmetry itself — not any single screen — is what makes a roach motel a dark pattern.

items.prompt: A pop-up asks users to subscribe to a newsletter. The decline option reads 'No thanks, I don't like saving money.' What pattern is this?
choices: Forced continuity
Confirmshaming — the decline option's label is worded to guilt or shame the user for choosing it
Hidden costs
Roach motel
items.explanation: Confirmshaming works by rewording the 'no' option itself to imply the user is making a foolish or bad choice, applying social/emotional pressure rather than presenting a genuine, neutral option. The manipulation is in the label's wording, not in hidden information.
items.reference:
A neutral decline reads 'No thanks'. Confirmshaming rewrites it as 'No, I don't want to save money' — same choice, engineered to feel foolish to pick.

Why: the manipulation lives entirely in how the 'no' option is worded, not in any information being hidden.

items.prompt: Which of these decline-button labels is an example of confirmshaming?
choices: "No thanks"
"Not now"
"No, I prefer to pay full price"
"Cancel"
items.explanation: "No, I prefer to pay full price" reframes a neutral decline as an admission of a bad decision — that's confirmshaming. The other three options state the choice neutrally, without an implied judgment attached to picking them.
items.reference:
A neutral decline reads 'No thanks'. Confirmshaming rewrites it as 'No, I don't want to save money' — same choice, engineered to feel foolish to pick.

Why: the manipulation lives entirely in how the 'no' option is worded, not in any information being hidden.

items.prompt: What is the defining feature of forced continuity, as distinct from just having a paid subscription?
choices: The subscription costs more than a competitor's
A free or trial offer converts to a recurring paid charge without a clear, timely warning the user is likely to actually see
The app requires an account to be created
The subscription auto-renews at all, regardless of notice given
items.explanation: Auto-renewal itself isn't the dark pattern — plenty of legitimate subscriptions renew automatically with clear notice. Forced continuity specifically means the warning is missing, too vague, or timed/placed to be easily missed, so the charge effectively happens without informed consent.
items.reference:
Auto-renewal + a clear, well-timed reminder = legitimate. Auto-renewal + a reminder timed or worded to be missed = forced continuity.

Why: the mechanism (auto-charge) is normal; what makes it a dark pattern is whether the warning was built to actually be seen.

items.prompt: A trial's only mention of its renewal date is a single line in the sign-up confirmation email, sent on day 1, with no follow-up reminder before the charge on day 14. Why is this forced continuity even though a renewal date was technically disclosed?
choices: It isn't — any disclosure, however placed, satisfies the requirement
Because the disclosure is timed and placed to be missed — a user has no reason to be looking for it on day 1, and nothing reminds them again before the charge
Because email is never a valid way to notify users of anything
Because trials should never require a card up front
items.explanation: A disclosure that technically exists but is engineered to be missed — wrong timing, no follow-up, buried in an email sent before the user has any reason to look for it — satisfies the letter of 'we told them' while defeating its purpose. That gap between technical disclosure and effective disclosure is the core of forced continuity.
items.reference:
Auto-renewal + a clear, well-timed reminder = legitimate. Auto-renewal + a reminder timed or worded to be missed = forced continuity.

Why: the mechanism (auto-charge) is normal; what makes it a dark pattern is whether the warning was built to actually be seen.

items.prompt: What does 'informed consent' mean in a UX context?
choices: The user clicked a button that says 'I agree'
The user's yes was given with accurate information, freely, and without engineered friction pushing them toward one answer
The terms of service were technically available somewhere on the site
A lawyer reviewed the flow before launch
items.explanation: Clicking 'I agree' or having terms exist somewhere doesn't establish informed consent on its own. Informed consent requires the information behind the decision to be accurate and actually visible, and the choice to be free of engineered pressure toward one outcome — a technically-present agreement obtained through hidden info or asymmetric friction isn't real consent.
items.reference:
Consent = accurate info + freely given + no engineered pressure. A click alone, or terms buried in fine print, satisfies none of these on its own.

Why: a 'yes' obtained through hidden information or asymmetric friction isn't real consent, even if a button was clicked.

items.prompt: Why do dark patterns matter beyond being annoying — what's the practical stake for a design that fails the informed-consent test?
choices: None — as long as users technically agreed, there's no real consequence
Several dark-pattern categories are now directly named and regulated (e.g. by EU and US rules) because manipulated consent isn't treated as real consent
It only matters for products aimed at children
It's purely a matter of taste or brand reputation, with no legal dimension
items.explanation: Regulators increasingly treat this as more than an ethics question — laws now name specific dark-pattern mechanisms (forced continuity, disproportionate cancellation friction, deceptive consent flows) as directly prohibited, because they treat consent obtained through manipulation as not being valid consent in the first place.
items.reference:
Consent = accurate info + freely given + no engineered pressure. A click alone, or terms buried in fine print, satisfies none of these on its own.

Why: a 'yes' obtained through hidden information or asymmetric friction isn't real consent, even if a button was clicked.

items.prompt: A fitness app's free trial requires a card up front and sends exactly one reminder email, timed to arrive 40 minutes before the trial converts, worded as a generic newsletter. Is this flow best described as clearly ethical or clearly a dark pattern?
choices: Clearly ethical — a reminder was sent, so disclosure requirements are met
It sits in a messy middle — no single piece is individually indefensible, but the cluster of choices (timing, wording, placement) all lean the same direction, away from the user noticing
Clearly a dark pattern — requiring a card for a trial is always manipulative
It can't be evaluated without knowing the exact subscription price
items.explanation: The spectrum from persuasion to manipulation has a genuine middle. A reminder existing, a card being required, and a fair price can each be individually justified — what makes this flow suspect is that every borderline choice (timing, subject line, inbox placement) points the same direction: away from the user noticing in time. A single borderline choice might be an oversight; a cluster that all lean the same way is a strategy.
items.reference:
One borderline choice ≈ oversight. Several borderline choices, all optimized the same direction ≈ strategy.

Why: individually-defensible pieces can still combine into a manipulative whole — evaluate the pattern of choices, not just each one in isolation.

items.prompt: Why is it a mistake to treat persuasion and manipulation as two clean, separate bins rather than a spectrum?
choices: Because manipulation doesn't actually exist as a category
Because real flows often combine several individually-defensible choices that only become manipulative in combination — a binary view misses that accumulation
Because persuasion is always ethical by definition
Because only lawyers are qualified to make this distinction
items.explanation: A strict binary view asks 'is this one screen manipulative, yes or no?' and often finds each screen individually defensible. The real risk lives in the combination — several borderline choices that all lean the same direction. Treating the question as a spectrum, and looking at the whole flow, catches what a screen-by-screen binary check misses.
items.reference:
One borderline choice ≈ oversight. Several borderline choices, all optimized the same direction ≈ strategy.

Why: individually-defensible pieces can still combine into a manipulative whole — evaluate the pattern of choices, not just each one in isolation.

items.prompt: The three-question test's first question asks whether the needed information is visible 'at the moment the user needs it.' Why does timing matter as much as whether the information exists at all?
choices: It doesn't — as long as information is disclosed somewhere, timing is irrelevant
Because information buried in terms or delivered after the decision window closes fails to actually inform the decision, even though it technically exists
Because users always read every notification regardless of timing
Because timing only matters for legal compliance, not for user experience
items.explanation: Information that exists but arrives too late, or is buried where the user isn't looking at decision time, doesn't functionally inform the decision — it only provides a technical alibi afterward. The test asks about visibility 'when needed' specifically to catch this gap between technical and effective disclosure.
items.reference:
Q1: Is info visible when needed?

Q2: Is effort symmetric?

Q3: Would the team disclose the mechanism aloud?

Why: a 'no' on two or three of these at once is where a design crosses from debatable nudge into dark pattern.

items.prompt: A pricing term is technically present in a 40-page terms-of-service document, but never shown on the checkout screen itself. Does this satisfy question 1 of the three-question test (info visible when needed)?
choices: Yes — anything present in the terms of service counts as disclosed
No — the information needs to be visible at the point of the actual decision, not merely present somewhere in a document the user isn't reading at that moment
Yes, but only if the terms of service were updated recently
The question doesn't apply to pricing, only to data collection
items.explanation: Question 1 specifically asks about visibility at decision time, not mere existence in a document. A fact buried in unread terms fails this test the same way the fitness app's vaguely-worded, poorly-timed reminder email did — it exists, but not where or when it can actually inform the choice.
items.reference:
Q1: Is info visible when needed?

Q2: Is effort symmetric?

Q3: Would the team disclose the mechanism aloud?

Why: a 'no' on two or three of these at once is where a design crosses from debatable nudge into dark pattern.

items.prompt: A subscription can be started in 2 clicks but requires navigating 4 screens with retention offers to cancel. Which of the three test questions does this most directly fail?
choices: Question 1 — visibility of information
Question 2 — whether effort is roughly symmetric between the two choices
Question 3 — willingness to disclose the mechanism
None of them — different flows are allowed to have different lengths
items.explanation: Question 2 asks specifically whether effort is symmetric between the choice that benefits the business (subscribing) and the choice that benefits the user (canceling). A 2-click sign-up against a 4-screen cancel is a direct, measurable asymmetry — this is the question it's designed to catch.
items.reference:
Q1: Is info visible when needed?

Q2: Is effort symmetric?

Q3: Would the team disclose the mechanism aloud?

Why: a 'no' on two or three of these at once is where a design crosses from debatable nudge into dark pattern.

items.prompt: Is a delete-confirmation dialog ('Are you sure? This can't be undone') automatically a dark pattern because it adds friction to an exit action?
choices: Yes — any added friction on an exit action is manipulative by definition
No — legitimate protective friction (like preventing an accidental destructive action) is a different shape than friction engineered specifically to suppress a metric like cancellations
Yes, but only if the dialog has more than one button
No, because confirmation dialogs are never considered friction at all
items.explanation: L2 explicitly distinguishes legitimate friction (a single, genuine confirmation protecting against mistakes) from a dark pattern's asymmetric friction (multiple screens, retention offers, and a shamed 'no' specifically to suppress cancellations). Not all friction is manipulative — the question is whether it protects the user or suppresses the business-costly choice.
items.reference:
Q1: Is info visible when needed?

Q2: Is effort symmetric?

Q3: Would the team disclose the mechanism aloud?

Why: a 'no' on two or three of these at once is where a design crosses from debatable nudge into dark pattern.

items.prompt: What does the third test question ('would the team be comfortable disclosing the mechanism out loud') actually check for?
choices: Whether the company has a public relations department
Whether the design would still seem acceptable if its actual mechanism were stated plainly to the users it targets, rather than left implicit
Whether the terms of service are written in plain language
Whether competitors use a similar design
items.explanation: This question is a gut-check: if a team wouldn't be willing to say 'we time the reminder to arrive 40 minutes before charging' out loud to their own users, that discomfort is itself a signal the mechanism relies on being unstated to work — which is a hallmark of manipulation rather than legitimate persuasion.
items.reference:
Q1: Is info visible when needed?

Q2: Is effort symmetric?

Q3: Would the team disclose the mechanism aloud?

Why: a 'no' on two or three of these at once is where a design crosses from debatable nudge into dark pattern.

items.prompt: An internal team openly documents a feature as 'best-sellers get a highlighted badge, based on real sales data.' What does this suggest about question 3 of the test?
choices: It fails question 3, because any internal documentation is suspicious
It passes question 3 — the team is comfortable naming the mechanism plainly, and it holds up when said out loud, unlike a euphemism hiding something else
Question 3 doesn't apply to features unrelated to cancellation
It's irrelevant to the test, which only concerns pricing
items.explanation: A mechanism a team can state plainly, without it reading as an admission of wrongdoing, passes question 3 — this is the signature of legitimate persuasion. Compare this to an internal code name for a deliberately long cancellation maze, which is itself evidence the team knew the mechanism wouldn't hold up if said out loud.
items.reference:
Q1: Is info visible when needed?

Q2: Is effort symmetric?

Q3: Would the team disclose the mechanism aloud?

Why: a 'no' on two or three of these at once is where a design crosses from debatable nudge into dark pattern.

items.prompt: A team under pressure to hit a 'retained subscribers' target proposes extending the cancel flow to 3 screens 'to give people a chance to reconsider.' What's the actual risk in evaluating this proposal only by whether the retention metric improves?
choices: There's no risk — any metric improvement is good for the business
A retention metric doesn't distinguish between the number improving because the offer got genuinely better versus because leaving got harder — only the three-question test tells those apart
The risk is purely that 3 screens takes longer to build than 1
There's no risk as long as legal approves the copy on each screen
items.explanation: A metric like 'retained subscribers' rewards any reduction in cancellations, regardless of cause. It can't tell the difference between users staying because a real, better offer changed their mind, and users staying because the exit got harder to navigate. Only running the three-question test on the actual flow distinguishes legitimate persuasion from friction added purely to suppress the number.
items.reference:
A metric moving is not evidence of how it moved. "Retention went up" is consistent with both a better offer and a harder exit.

Why: business metrics reward outcomes, not mechanisms — the three-question test is what checks the mechanism.

items.prompt: If the 3 added cancel screens in the scenario above actually presented new, true, useful information (e.g. an accurate summary of unused entitlements the user would lose), how would that affect the evaluation?
choices: It wouldn't matter — any added screen before cancellation is automatically manipulative
It would likely satisfy question 1 (informing the user better) and could be legitimate, provided effort still stays reasonably symmetric and the mechanism would hold up disclosed
It would only matter if the information were shown after the cancellation was already confirmed
It's irrelevant since informed consent only applies to data collection, not subscriptions
items.explanation: The three-question test doesn't ban all friction — it asks what the friction accomplishes. Screens that provide genuinely new, accurate information satisfy question 1 and can be legitimate persuasion, as long as they don't also fail question 2 (disproportionate effort) or question 3 (a mechanism the team wouldn't want to say out loud).
items.reference:
A metric moving is not evidence of how it moved. "Retention went up" is consistent with both a better offer and a harder exit.

Why: business metrics reward outcomes, not mechanisms — the three-question test is what checks the mechanism.

items.prompt: Why is 'legitimate friction, like a delete confirmation' a genuinely different shape from 'friction added to suppress a metric,' even though both add steps before an exit action?
choices: They aren't different — all added friction before an exit is equally suspect

Legitimate friction protects the user from an accidental mistake and stays proportionate; metric-driven friction escalates specifically to make the disfavored choice harder, often paired with a shamed or shrunk 'no'
The only real difference is which department designed the screen
Legitimate friction is always exactly one screen, and manipulative friction is always more than one
items.explanation: A single, genuine confirmation ('are you sure, this can't be undone') protects against accidental action and stops there. Metric-driven friction, by contrast, tends to escalate (multiple screens, retention offers, a shamed decline) specifically in the direction that suppresses the measured outcome — the number of steps alone doesn't distinguish them, but the pattern and purpose do.
items.reference:
A metric moving is not evidence of how it moved. "Retention went up" is consistent with both a better offer and a harder exit.

Why: business metrics reward outcomes, not mechanisms — the three-question test is what checks the mechanism.

items.prompt: A checkout page shows a bright 'Add protection plan — recommended' button and, in the same-size text and same color, a plain 'skip' link right next to it. Applying the three-question test, does this pass or fail?
choices: It fails outright, since any upsell during checkout is manipulative

It's a reasonable pass — the offer is visible and true, the decline is the same size and color as the accept (symmetric effort/visibility), and the mechanism ('we recommend add-ons') would hold up disclosed
It fails, because the word 'recommended' is inherently deceptive
It can't be evaluated without knowing the exact price of the protection plan
items.explanation: This is a useful contrast case: the offer is visible and truthful, and — critically — the decline option isn't shrunk, hidden, or worded to shame the user. Same-size, same-color options with a neutral 'skip' label keep effort and visibility symmetric, which is what separates this from the confirmshaming and roach-motel examples earlier in the unit.
items.reference:
Contrast case: a true, visible offer with a neutral, equally-sized decline passes all three questions — it's the shape, not the presence of an upsell, that matters.

Why: recognizing a passing case is as important as recognizing a failing one — the test isn't 'no upsells ever.'

items.prompt: A settings toggle for 'share my data with partners' is pre-checked (on) by default, and turning it off requires expanding a collapsed 'advanced' section first. What does this fail, and why?
choices: Nothing — defaults are a normal, neutral part of design and users can always change them
It fails question 1 and question 2 — the opt-out is hidden behind an extra step (collapsed section) that the opt-in doesn't require, making the 'no' harder to find and act on than the 'yes'
It fails only because pre-checked boxes are illegal everywhere
It fails question 3 only, since the mechanism would be fine to disclose
items.explanation: A pre-checked default paired with an extra, hidden step to reverse it fails both visibility (the opt-out isn't where the user would look) and symmetry (opting in required zero effort; opting out requires finding and expanding a hidden section). This is a common, low-key version of the same asymmetric-effort shape seen in the unit's bigger cases.
items.reference:
Contrast case: a true, visible offer with a neutral, equally-sized decline passes all three questions — it's the shape, not the presence of an upsell, that matters.

Why: recognizing a passing case is as important as recognizing a failing one — the test isn't 'no upsells ever.'

items.prompt: In the documented case where a subscription's cancellation flow required navigating several screens of discounts, and the company defended it by saying each offer contained real, true information, what's the flaw in that defense under the three-question test?
choices: There's no flaw — true offers can never be part of a dark pattern

The offers being true addresses question 1, but the flow still failed question 2 (disproportionate effort vs. 2-click sign-up) and question 3 (an internal code name referencing a long siege suggests the team knew the friction was intentional)
The defense is irrelevant because discounts are always illegal to offer during cancellation
The flaw is that the discounts should have been larger
items.explanation: Each question in the test is independent — passing one doesn't clear the whole flow. True offer content can satisfy question 1 while the flow still fails on effort symmetry and on whether the team would be comfortable disclosing the mechanism (an internal reference to a legendarily long siege is itself evidence against question 3).
items.reference:
Q1 visible?Partial — offers true, but 'cancel' worded ambiguously, placed last
Q2 symmetric?No — 2-click signup vs. multi-screen exit
Q3 disclose?No — internal code name evidences intent

Why: true content on one screen doesn't rescue a flow that fails the other two questions.

items.prompt: What is the core redesign principle applied to fix the multi-screen cancellation maze described in this unit?
choices: Remove all retention offers entirely, since any offer is inherently manipulative
Give cancel a single, clearly labeled control reachable in the same effort as sign-up; a retention offer can appear once, clearly labeled, with a real, unshamed decline
Add legal disclaimers to every screen so users can't claim they weren't warned
Require a phone call to confirm cancellation intent, to reduce accidental cancellations
items.explanation: The fix isn't to eliminate persuasion — a retention offer can still ethically appear. The fix is to restore symmetry: cancel reachable in comparable effort to sign-up, one offer shown clearly (not buried in a maze), and a decline option that isn't shrunk or worded to shame the user for choosing it.
items.reference:
Q1 visible?Partial — offers true, but 'cancel' worded ambiguously, placed last
Q2 symmetric?No — 2-click signup vs. multi-screen exit
Q3 disclose?No — internal code name evidences intent

Why: true content on one screen doesn't rescue a flow that fails the other two questions.

items.prompt: The trial-to-bill case's refund process routes requests through a support ticket queue with a 5-7 business day response time. Why does this detail matter to the ethical evaluation, beyond the missed reminder itself?
choices: It doesn't matter — refund speed is unrelated to informed consent
It compounds the harm: even a user who does notice the charge quickly is likely to miss their bank's dispute window before a slow refund process responds, closing off their remaining recourse
It matters only because 5-7 days violates a specific numerical legal limit
It's actually a point in the company's favor, since a refund process exists at all
items.explanation: A slow refund process isn't a separate issue — it's part of the same pattern. Even a user who catches the charge quickly needs a fast path to reverse it before their bank's 'recognized charge' dispute window closes; a multi-day ticket queue quietly bets against most users making that window, extending the harm caused by the missed reminder.
items.reference:
Fix: renewal date/price shown inside the product (persistent banner), a plain billing-worded reminder 2-3 days out, and automatic refunds within a short post-charge window.

Why: the whole point of a trial is a real chance to decide — a slow refund path quietly shortens that chance after the fact.

items.prompt: What does the L3 redesign of the trial-to-bill flow add, beyond a better-timed email reminder?
choices: Nothing else is needed once the email is fixed
A persistent, dismissible in-product banner showing the renewal date and price, plus an automatic (not ticket-queue) refund for charges disputed within a short window after billing
A requirement that all trials must be permanently free
Removing the card requirement at signup entirely
items.explanation: The redesign addresses both ends of the problem: making the renewal fact visible inside the product itself (not just a one-time email), and making the recourse fast if a user does get charged unexpectedly (automatic refund in a short window, not a multi-day ticket queue) — since the trial's entire premise is giving the user a genuine chance to decide.
items.reference:
Fix: renewal date/price shown inside the product (persistent banner), a plain billing-worded reminder 2-3 days out, and automatic refunds within a short post-charge window.

Why: the whole point of a trial is a real chance to decide — a slow refund path quietly shortens that chance after the fact.

items.prompt: A rewards program can be joined with one tap, but leaving requires calling a business-hours-only phone line and providing a member ID never shown in the app. What makes this case notable compared to Case 1 and Case 2?
choices: It isn't notable — it's identical to Case 1 in every respect
It applies the same fast-in/slow-out shape to personal data and account existence rather than money, which is exactly the shape targeted by state privacy laws around consent for data collection
It's notable only because it involves a phone call
It's the least serious case because no money changes hands
items.explanation: Case 1 and 2 center on money (subscription cancellation, billing). Case 3 applies the same roach-motel and hidden-cost shapes to personal data and account deletion — an area several state privacy laws now specifically regulate, treating manipulated consent for data collection as its own violation, separate from any financial harm.
items.reference:
Roach motel1-tap in, phone-call-only out
Hidden costMember ID never shown in-app

Why: the same dark-pattern shapes apply beyond money — to personal data and account control, which is exactly what several privacy laws now target.

items.prompt: In Case 3, what specifically plays the role of a 'hidden cost,' given that the rewards program itself is free?
choices: The retail chain's product prices
Information the user needs to leave (the member ID) that's never surfaced anywhere in the app they actually use
The tax charged on rewards points
There is no hidden cost in this case, only a roach motel
items.explanation: A 'hidden cost' doesn't have to be money — it's whatever necessary resource is withheld until the last, least convenient moment. Here it's information: the member ID required to exit is never shown in the app itself, so the user has to separately locate it before they can even attempt the phone-based deletion process.
items.reference:
Roach motel1-tap in, phone-call-only out
Hidden costMember ID never shown in-app

Why: the same dark-pattern shapes apply beyond money — to personal data and account control, which is exactly what several privacy laws now target.

items.prompt: In the trial-to-bill case, the terms of service technically state the renewal date. Why does that fact alone not make the flow ethical under the three-question test?
choices: It does make the flow ethical — any stated term, anywhere, is sufficient

Because question 1 asks whether the info is visible when the user needs it, not whether it exists in a document somewhere — a date stated once in fine print, with no follow-up reminder, fails that bar
Because terms of service are not legally binding documents
Because the flow only becomes unethical once a refund is actually denied
items.explanation: This mirrors the earlier fitness-app example: a technically-present disclosure that isn't positioned or timed to actually reach the user at decision time fails question 1's real bar, which is effective visibility, not mere existence in a document.

items.prompt: What do the FTC's click-to-cancel rule, the EU's Digital Services Act dark-pattern provisions, and state privacy laws have in common in how they evaluate a flow?
choices: They all require proving the company's exact internal intent through documents

They look at the shape of the flow — whether exiting is harder than entering, whether disclosure is timed to be missed, whether consent came through confusion — the same shape the three-question test checks
They only apply to companies above a certain revenue threshold
They require every dark pattern to be reported to a regulator before launch
items.explanation: None of these rules require reading minds about intent — they evaluate the observable structure of the flow itself: is exiting harder than entering, is disclosure timed to be missed, is consent obtained through confusion. That's exactly what the three-question test evaluates too, which is why running it pre-launch catches the same issues a regulator would later flag.

items.prompt: A team argues 'ethics is subjective, so as long as legal hasn't flagged our flow, it's fine.' What's the flaw in treating 'not yet flagged' as equivalent to 'compliant'?
choices: There's no flaw — legal review is the only meaningful check that matters

'Not yet flagged' often just means 'not yet caught' — waiting for enforcement treats regulators as the detection mechanism instead of design review, while user harm and reputational damage happen immediately and continuously in the meantime

There's no flaw, because dark pattern law hasn't changed in decades
items.explanation: Regulatory enforcement is slow and reactive by nature; a flow can ship harm to real users for a long time before it's caught. Design review that runs the three-question test proactively catches the same shape enforcement targets, before it ships — treating 'not yet flagged' as 'fine' just means outsourcing detection to whoever notices last.

items.prompt: Why does the FTC's click-to-cancel rule specifically target the shape seen in Case 1 (the multi-screen cancellation maze)?
choices: Because that shape (easy sign-up, disproportionately hard cancellation) is precisely the asymmetric-effort pattern the rule requires companies to eliminate — cancellation must be at least as easy as sign-up

items.prompt: Across all three worked cases in this unit, what's the single redesign principle that recurs in every fix?
choices: Remove all persuasive elements from the product entirely
Restore rough symmetry — make the exit/decline path require comparable effort and comparable information visibility to the entry/accept path
Add more legal disclaimers to every screen
Require a human support agent to approve every action
items.explanation: Every redesign in this unit follows the same logic: not eliminating persuasion, but restoring the symmetry the three-question test checks for — comparable effort and comparable information visibility between the path that benefits the business and the path that benefits the user, whether that's canceling, exiting a trial, or deleting an account.
items.reference:
Case 1: cancel matches signup effort. Case 2: renewal visible in-product + fast refunds. Case 3: deletion doesn't require info unavailable in-app.

Why: every fix targets the same root cause — asymmetric effort or visibility between the two paths, not the presence of persuasion itself.

items.prompt: A team redesigning a cancellation flow removes the maze but adds a single, clearly-labeled retention offer with a real, unshamed decline option. Does this redesign still count as ethical persuasion, or has it become a dark pattern again?
choices: It's automatically a dark pattern, since any retention offer during cancellation is inherently manipulative
It's still legitimate persuasion — a single, clearly labeled offer with a real, easy decline satisfies all three test questions, unlike the original multi-screen, shamed-decline maze
It depends entirely on the size of the discount offered
It's illegal under all major dark-pattern regulations regardless of presentation
items.explanation: The three-question test doesn't ban persuasion or retention offers — it targets structure. A single offer, clearly labeled as an offer, with a decline option that's genuinely easy and unshamed, passes all three questions: the offer is visible and true, effort stays symmetric, and the team could disclose it plainly. That's the difference between this redesign and the original maze.

items.prompt: The unit closes by asking what changes if a flow asks someone to leave a support group or a political opt-in list, rather than a paid subscription. Why might the same three-question test need a stricter bar in that context?
choices: It wouldn't need a stricter bar — money and non-monetary harm are always equivalent

Because the harm from friction on exit isn't a wasted charge that can be refunded, but potentially something the user can't easily undo the effect of at all — the stakes of getting the exit wrong are qualitatively different
Because support groups and political lists are never allowed to have any exit friction whatsoever

items.explanation: A wasted subscription charge is bad but reversible — a refund resolves it. Friction that delays or discourages leaving a support group or a political data list can cause harm that isn't reversible the same way (continued unwanted contact, ongoing data exposure, social pressure). The same test questions still apply, but what counts as an acceptable 'no' on any of them may need to be stricter when the downside of getting it wrong isn't easily undone.
